offtopic: I finally figured out why my rice kept sticking. Turning the heat down actually helps, apparently. I've been scraping that pot for months.
My bus went past the stop this morning, so I got an unexpected walk before work. At least the weather was decent for once.
I started that detective show and immediately guessed the wrong suspect. I'm three episodes in and still backing my terrible original theory.
Made soup with whatever was left in the fridge. It looks pretty questionable, but I packed a second serving for tomorrow anyway.
I keep losing the same screwdriver halfway through assembling this shelf. It has spent more time under the couch than in my hand.
The bakery near my stop has these little cheese rolls now. I went in for bread and came home with six rolls and no bread.

items.post_a: I think a painting can be beautiful even if nobody ever sees it. Its artistic quality belongs to the work itself; an empty gallery doesn't somehow switch that quality off.
items.post_b: I've changed my mind about beauty being there all by itself. I now think artistic worth comes from how people experience a work. Without any possible audience response, there's no aesthetic value waiting inside it.
fillers: That forgotten mural still has artistic merit, as far as I'm concerned. Getting ignored doesn't remove the quality it already has, any more than getting popular automatically adds quality.
I don't think everyone disliking a sculpture would settle whether it's good art. People can miss something that's actually there in the piece, including its beauty.
items.note: B explicitly announces a change and adopts response-dependent aesthetic value.

items.post_a: I don't buy a final stopping point where something just happens for absolutely no reason. For any fact, I think there's an explanation, even if we'll never manage to find it.
items.post_b: I'm less confident that every fact needs an explanation these days. The idea of something just being the case has more pull than it used to, but I haven't decided that any facts actually lack explanations.
fillers: When someone says the initial conditions just were that way, I still want to ask why. I think there's an answer behind those conditions too, whether or not we're equipped to uncover it.
My ignorance about why something happened isn't a feature of the thing itself. I take unexplained facts to be gaps in our understanding, with an explanation there to be found.
items.note: B questions confidence in universal explanation without endorsing brute facts.

items.post_a: I judge an action by how things turn out for everyone affected. The right move is whichever option brings about the best total result, even when that means breaking a familiar rule.
items.post_b: I think doing the right thing starts with our duties and other people's rights. Those are binding even when ignoring them would produce a better overall result; a good payoff doesn't make a violation right.
fillers: If telling a lie would genuinely leave everyone better off than telling the truth, I'd call the lie right. For me, the final balance of consequences is what decides it.
I treat moral rules as useful shortcuts for getting good results. When following a rule would give a worse outcome than another available choice, I think we should choose the better outcome.
items.note: B directly adopts duties and rights regardless of consequences, reversing A.

items.post_a: I think everything we actually know about the world ultimately comes through experience. Reason helps organize the material, but it can't supply substantive knowledge of reality without anything coming in through the senses.
items.post_b: The author I was reading argues that thinking alone can reveal substantial truths about reality, without sensory input. I'm describing her position here, not signing onto it; I still need experience doing the grounding work.
fillers: Even when I work something out from my desk, the premises about the world came from observation somewhere along the way. I don't see that as knowledge springing from pure thought.
I can imagine a perfectly tidy argument about how nature works and still need evidence that its starting points are true. My view is that worldly knowledge always traces back to sensory contact.
items.note: B attributes reason-alone knowledge to an author and explicitly withholds adoption.

items.post_a: My kitchen light finally stopped flickering after I replaced the bulb, which feels like a major household achievement this week. I think researchers could keep ethical and political priorities out of their reasoning, but should deliberately include them. Anyway, I spent the rest of the evening making pasta and trying to get a stain out of my favorite sweater before it dried.
items.post_b: I took the long route home because the usual sidewalk was blocked again, and ended up finding a tiny grocery store with excellent peaches. I think ethical and political priorities inevitably enter scientific reasoning, even when researchers try to exclude them. The peaches survived the walk better than the bread did; I really need to stop packing everything in the same bag.
fillers: I spent most of Saturday reorganizing the hallway cupboard and found three umbrellas I'd completely forgotten about. My take is that scientific reasoning can leave social and ethical priorities aside, but ought to give them a deliberate role. After lunch I tried hanging a little hook for the umbrellas, discovered the wall was harder than expected, and abandoned the project until I can borrow a drill.

The new cafe has decent coffee, though the chairs are somehow less comfortable than the bus seats outside. I believe scientists have the option of reasoning without moral or political considerations, yet should choose to bring those considerations in. I stayed long enough to finish my sandwich, then went home to deal with the laundry I'd left sitting in the machine all morning.
items.note: Amid unrelated errands, B makes values unavoidable where A says their inclusion is optional.

offtopic: I tried growing basil on the windowsill again. This plant has lasted eleven days, which already puts it ahead of my previous attempts.
My headphones only work if the cable sits at a very specific angle. I spent the whole train ride holding my phone like a tiny tray.
I bought the wrong size bedsheet and somehow didn't notice until the third corner. The packaging is already shredded, so that's a fun little problem.
There's a new shortcut in the game I've been playing, but I crash every time I attempt it. Taking the regular route would be faster by now.
I made pancakes for dinner because I forgot to shop. Added frozen berries and ended up pretty pleased with the whole accidental arrangement.
The neighbors moved their piano away from our shared wall. I can still hear it, but now it sounds like background music instead of a personal concert.

items.post_a: I think a belief can be justified because the process producing it is dependable, even if I can't inspect that dependability from inside my own head. Reflection doesn't have to expose every relevant factor.
items.post_b: For me, having good grounds can involve a trustworthy mental process that I'm unable to explain or examine. Whether I'm justified isn't settled entirely by what introspection lets me get at.
fillers: I trust a normal visual judgment even when I can't give myself an internal demonstration that my vision works reliably. I think that actual reliability can help justify the belief all the same.

Two people could feel equally certain while only one has a dependable way of forming the belief. I think that difference can matter to justification, even when neither person can reflectively spot it.
items.note: B repeats that justification may depend on inaccessible reliability.

items.post_a: I see time as events standing in earlier and later relations. Calling this bit now tells you where I'm speaking from; I don't think there's an extra cosmic spotlight picking out one special moment.
items.post_b: I'm wavering on whether earlier and later relations tell the whole story. An objectively special now is starting to seem tempting, but I'm still undecided about whether reality actually has one.
fillers: When I look at a calendar, I think my position changes which date I call today. There's no additional fact making that date universally present; the ordering of events does all the work.
I don't think the universe needs a moving present on top of its temporal arrangement. Events occurring before or after each other are enough, with now working like here does for location.
items.note: B expresses uncertainty and attraction to Y without adopting an objective present.

items.post_a: I managed to spill tea over the craft table before we'd even started, so most of the session involved paper towels and moving everyone's supplies. I think the clay figure and the lump it's made from are simply one object described in different ways. We eventually got the table dry, put some music on, and finished a tray of biscuits while waiting for the kettle.
items.post_b: My parcel arrived just as I was leaving, which meant carrying a ridiculous cardboard box on the bus and getting stared at all the way downtown. I think a clay sculpture and its underlying lump are two separate objects occupying exactly the same space. The parcel was only a replacement lampshade, and after all that trouble it turned out to be slightly too wide for the fitting.
fillers: I tried fixing the loose handle on the cupboard today and dropped a screw straight into the heating vent. As I see it, shaping a lump into a statue leaves us with one thing under two descriptions. The handle is still loose, the screw is still missing, and I've put a piece of tape over the vent so the next attempt doesn't end the same way.

The pottery room was freezing this morning, and I kept my jacket on until someone finally worked out the heater controls. I count the clay and the statue formed from it as a single object, however we happen to describe it. After class I stopped for noodles, missed my usual bus, and ended up walking home with the leftovers balanced on top of my bag.
items.note: B buries a two-object view in everyday narrative, contradicting A's one-object view.

items.post_a: I think some things make a life meaningful whether the person values them or not. Caring for someone can matter in that way even if the caregiver feels bored and wishes they were elsewhere.
items.post_b: My friend says meaning comes wholly from whatever a person cares about or decides to pursue. I can explain why that appeals to him, but it isn't my position; I still think some activities matter independently.
fillers: Someone could dismiss years of helping others as pointless, and I think those years could still give their life meaning. Their own assessment isn't the only thing that determines whether it mattered.

I don't think a worthwhile discovery loses its contribution to someone's life just because they stop caring about it. At least some sources of meaning hold up independently of the person's preferences.
items.note: B reports a friend's attitude-dependent account while retaining A's view.

items.post_a: I think careful reasoning can sometimes tell us substantial things about reality without relying on sensory evidence. Observation is useful, obviously, but I don't believe every bit of worldly knowledge has to start there.
items.post_b: I still think pure thought can get us genuine knowledge about how the world must be. We don't always need something seen, heard, or touched as the ultimate basis for knowing it.
fillers: I don't see armchair reasoning as limited to shuffling definitions. I think it can reveal something substantive about reality itself, even when no observation supplies the grounds for the conclusion.
My view is that thinking something through can occasionally reach beyond our concepts and establish a truth about the world. Sensory experience isn't a necessary starting point for every such truth.
items.note: B restates the possibility of substantive knowledge through reason alone.

offtopic: I keep bringing too many snacks on hikes. We were out for two hours and I had enough crackers for an overnight trip.
The washing machine makes a new clicking sound during the spin cycle. I checked the pockets and found a coin, but the clicking survived.
I replayed the first level to find one missing collectible and accidentally stayed up until two. Still missing it, which makes the whole thing worse.
My homemade pizza came out shaped like a boot. The crust was good though, and the narrow end made a convenient handle.
I got to the pool early and had a whole lane to myself. By the time everyone else arrived I'd already worn myself out.
Bought a cheap desk lamp and now I can actually see the keyboard at night. Should have done that before spending months squinting at it.

items.post_a: I think believing or wanting something is basically having certain tendencies: how I'd act, what I'd think, and how I'd feel in relevant situations. Those patterns are what the attitudes amount to.
items.post_b: Could beliefs and desires instead be connections to little representations inside the mind? I'm asking how that account works, not endorsing it: what would make one internal representation a belief rather than a wish?
fillers: When I say I want a day off, I mean a whole pattern of readiness to plan for it, feel relieved about it, and choose it. I take that pattern to constitute the desire.

To me, believing the bridge is unsafe consists in tendencies to avoid it, worry about crossing, and reason accordingly. It's the organized pattern of thinking, feeling, and acting that makes it a belief.
items.note: B asks about mental representations and explicitly does not endorse that account.

items.post_a: I think arguments about what exists can be about serious features of reality. Getting our words straight isn't enough; the world itself settles whether the disputed things are actually there.
items.post_b: If existence questions really could be settled just by sorting out our concepts and language, I'd expect a lot of these debates to end pretty quickly. That's a hypothetical consequence, not a claim that the premise is true.
fillers: I don't think defining a term settles whether the corresponding thing exists. My view is that there's a substantial answer fixed by reality, and the definition alone doesn't deliver it.

When philosophers disagree about which objects there are, I think they can be disagreeing about the world's actual structure. Some of those arguments need discoveries about reality, beyond clarification of vocabulary.
items.note: B considers what would follow from Y while explicitly treating it as hypothetical.

items.post_a: I think the continuum hypothesis has a fixed truth value, even if our usual axioms don't settle it. There's a definite answer about whether an infinite size sits between the integers and reals.
items.post_b: For me, mathematical reality leaves that gap unsettled: neither alternative wins absolutely. Choosing a framework supplies a verdict within it, but doesn't uncover an independently settled yes or no.
fillers: Independence from a set of axioms doesn't convince me the continuum hypothesis is genuinely open in reality. I think one answer is correct, whether or not our present tools can establish which.

I take the question of an intermediate infinity to have an answer already. Our inability to prove the continuum hypothesis or its negation from familiar assumptions is a limitation on those assumptions.
items.note: B uses different vocabulary to deny a determinate answer without announcing a change.

items.post_a: The clock above the pool was broken again, so I counted laps until my arms got tired and hoped I hadn't missed the bus. I think there's a real, observer-independent fact about which moment is happening now. I made it to the stop with damp hair and one glove missing, then spent the whole ride trying to remember where I'd put the other one.
items.post_b: I spent the evening putting old photos into folders, which took forever because half the files had useless names and several were duplicates. I think all there is to time is how events stand earlier or later than each other, without an objectively privileged present. I eventually gave up sorting the holiday pictures and made toast, then discovered I'd left the butter out since breakfast.
fillers: My oven timer went off while I was on the phone, and by the time I got to the kitchen the edges of dinner were pretty dark. I believe reality singles out a particular moment as present, regardless of anyone's perspective. I scraped off the worst bits, opened a window, and spent the rest of the evening hoping the burnt smell wouldn't get into my coat.

I tried taking the earlier train this morning and found out the station cafe doesn't open until after it leaves. My view is that which moment is now belongs to the world itself, independently of how we describe it. I ate the emergency granola bar from my bag, read a few chapters on the journey, and arrived with enough time to buy a proper breakfast.
items.note: B embeds a relational-only account of time that reverses A's objective present.

items.post_a: I think natural selection primarily sorts whole organisms. It's the animal or plant as a functioning package that survives and reproduces, so that's the main unit I see selection acting on.
items.post_b: I used to put the whole organism at the center, but I've changed my mind. I now think genes are the basic units of natural selection; their differential continuation is what ultimately drives the process.
fillers: A trait has to work as part of a living creature facing its environment. That's why I regard the complete organism as the primary target of selection, rather than treating each inherited component separately.
When I picture selection in a drought, I picture entire plants making it or failing and leaving different numbers of offspring. To me, those integrated individuals are the main units being selected.
items.note: B explicitly changes from organism-centered to gene-centered selection.

offtopic: I tried a different route to the supermarket and found a much quieter street. Slightly longer walk, but I didn't have to dodge delivery bikes.
My controller started drifting during the final race. I still finished, but mostly by steering hard enough in the opposite direction to make my thumb ache.
I cooked way too many potatoes again. Tomorrow's lunch is sorted, and probably the lunch after that if I can find another clean container.
The shower finally has decent pressure after the repair. I was late getting ready because I stayed in there enjoying it longer than planned.
I went to return one library book and borrowed four more. My bedside table is getting crowded, but at least the weather forecast looks rainy.
Found my missing scarf inside a pillowcase while folding laundry. I'd already searched every coat pocket twice and blamed the bus at least once.

items.post_a: I'd take both boxes in Newcomb's problem. The predictor has already put the money in or left it out, so grabbing the visible thousand improves my haul either way. That's the rational move to me.
items.post_b: I've switched sides on Newcomb's problem. I now think taking just the opaque box is the rational choice: with that reliable predictor, the people who choose it alone are the ones walking away rich.
fillers: My decision in Newcomb would be to collect both containers. Once I'm standing there, the hidden amount is fixed, and I see no rational reason to leave an extra thousand sitting on the table.
I know the prediction is supposed to be excellent, but I'd still pick both in Newcomb. Whichever amount is already hidden, adding the clear box raises my payout, so that's what I consider rational.
items.note: B announces switching sides and endorses one-boxing over A's two-boxing.

items.post_a: I think my mental states stay inside my brain and body. A notebook can help me remember things, but it's an external aid rather than an actual piece of my mind.
items.post_b: I'd count a routinely consulted phone as literally helping constitute someone's cognition. For me, thinking can genuinely span a person and their equipment, instead of ending at the skin.
fillers: Losing my diary would make remembering appointments harder, but I wouldn't say a part of my mind had gone missing. I locate mental states within the person, even when tools are useful.
I can rely heavily on a map without its markings becoming part of a mental state. In my view, the cognition itself remains in my brain and body; the map supports it from outside.
items.note: B adopts externally constituted cognition using different content words and no change signal.

items.post_a: I think some collections of things make a further object and others don't. Parts assembled into a bicycle qualify; a random selection of scattered stuff doesn't automatically add one more thing to the world.
items.post_b: I've changed my mind about composition needing special conditions. I now think any assortment whatsoever forms another object, including wildly scattered bits. Being an odd or useless whole doesn't stop it from existing.
fillers: I don't think every arbitrary grouping creates an additional object. Some parts really combine into a whole, but I take composition to occur selectively, rather than whenever we can list some things together.
Calling a pebble and a distant cloud a collection doesn't convince me there's a further object made of them. I think composition happens in some cases, like an integrated chair, and fails in others.
items.note: B explicitly changes from selective to unrestricted composition.

items.post_a: I count the statue and its clay as one thing. Describing it as a lump focuses on the material, while calling it a statue focuses on the shape; that doesn't double the objects there.
items.post_b: I still only count a single object on the sculptor's stand. The material lump just is the sculpture, even though the two descriptions highlight different features of what I'm looking at.
fillers: If I buy a clay statue, I don't think I've acquired two overlapping possessions. For me, the lump that was shaped and the artwork sitting there are numerically the same object.
I can talk about what the clay weighs or what the statue depicts without introducing two things. My view is that it's one object doing both jobs in those descriptions.
items.note: B repeats A's identification of the statue with the clay.

items.post_a: The dishwasher stopped halfway through its cycle last night, and I spent a while moving wet plates around before finding the instruction booklet. I think every fact has some explanation, even if nobody can discover it. After getting the machine going again, I reheated dinner and watched the second half of a film I'd started days ago, though I barely remembered what had happened in the first half.
items.post_b: I took a bag of old clothes to the donation bin this morning and somehow came back carrying a secondhand lamp from the shop next door. I think some facts have no explanation at all and are simply how reality is. The lamp works, but the shade is crooked, so I spent the afternoon adjusting it before giving up and moving it to the corner of the room.
fillers: My upstairs neighbor was moving furniture before breakfast, so I gave up sleeping in and went out for a bagel while the street was still quiet. I believe there's a reason behind every fact, including ones we'll never be able to account for ourselves. The bagel place had changed its menu, and I spent far too long choosing before ordering exactly what I usually get.

I finally cleaned the crumbs out of my keyboard and found a surprising amount of cat hair for someone who doesn't own a cat. As I see it, anything that's the case has an explanation, however far beyond our reach that explanation might be. Once the keys were back on, I tested them by typing a shopping list and realized I'd forgotten to buy most of dinner.
items.note: B buries an endorsement of brute facts, contradicting A's universal explanation.
